subject: cli
title: Reveal hidden files
prompt: Complete ls so it includes entries whose names begin with a dot.
explanation: The -a flag includes hidden entries. GNU ls also accepts --all. Flags are case-sensitive: -A is related but excludes . and ...
hint: The short flag is a lowercase a.

subject: cli
title: Where am I?
prompt: Enter the Bash command that prints the current working directory.
explanation: pwd prints the full path of the directory the shell is currently in. It does not change directories.
hint: The name abbreviates print working directory.

subject: cli
title: Inspect the start of a log
prompt: Complete head to print the first 5 lines of access.log.
explanation: head reads the beginning of a file. -n 5 selects five lines; access.log is the filename.
hint: Use -n followed by the number of lines.

subject: cli
title: Find log files
prompt: Complete find to locate regular files under /var/log whose names end in .log. Quote the filename pattern so the shell does not expand it.
explanation: -type f restricts results to regular files. -name matches the filename; quoting *.log leaves the wildcard for find to interpret.
hint: Combine -type f with -name and a quoted pattern.

subject: cli
title: Show every entry
prompt: Complete CMD dir to include hidden and system entries as well as ordinary files.
explanation: CMD uses slash-prefixed switches. /a without an attribute filter includes all attributes, including hidden and system entries.
hint: Use the all-attributes switch.

subject: cli
title: Change drive and directory
prompt: Complete CMD cd to change both the active drive and directory to D:\data.
explanation: The /d switch changes the current drive as well as its current directory. Without it, cd can update another drive's saved directory without switching drives.
hint: Start with /d, then provide the complete path.

subject: cli
title: Inspect processes in CMD
prompt: Enter the CMD utility that lists running processes.
explanation: tasklist lists processes, including their image names and process IDs. This card specifically asks for the CMD utility.
hint: Its name combines task and list.

subject: cli
title: Find the newest entries
prompt: Complete CMD dir to include all entries, search subdirectories, and sort each listing by date with newest first.
explanation: /a includes all entries; /s searches subdirectories; /o-d reverses date order. /od would put the oldest entries first.
hint: The date sort key is d; a preceding minus reverses it.

subject: cli
title: Reveal hidden items in PowerShell
prompt: Complete Get-ChildItem so it also lists hidden items in the current directory.
explanation: -Force includes items that are normally hidden from this listing. It does not bypass permissions.
hint: The parameter is named Force.

subject: cli
title: Read the end of a log
prompt: Complete Get-Content to return only the last 5 lines of app.log.
explanation: -Path supplies the file. -Tail 5 requests the last five lines, which is useful for a quick look at recent log entries.
hint: Use the Tail parameter and a line count.

subject: cli
title: Inspect processes in PowerShell
prompt: Enter the full PowerShell cmdlet name that returns running processes.
explanation: Get-Process returns process objects. Later commands can select properties or filter these objects. This exercise asks for the full cmdlet name.
hint: PowerShell cmdlets follow the Verb-Noun naming pattern.

subject: cli
title: Select log files in PowerShell
prompt: Complete Get-ChildItem to return regular files in the current directory whose names match *.log.
explanation: -File excludes directories. -Filter passes the wildcard pattern to the filesystem provider. The pattern is not a regular expression.
hint: Combine the File switch and a Filter wildcard.

subject: regex
title: Match one whole word
prompt: Match the complete lowercase string cat, and nothing before or after it. Enter the pattern without / delimiters.
explanation: ^ anchors the start and $ anchors the end. Without anchors, cat would also match a substring of scatter.
hint: Put an anchor on each side of cat.

subject: regex
title: Recognize digits
prompt: Complete the pattern to match a nonempty string containing only ASCII digits.
explanation: In JavaScript, \d matches an ASCII digit. + requires at least one. \D means a non-digit and is not interchangeable.
hint: A digit class followed by a one-or-more quantifier.

subject: regex
title: Recognize an order ID
prompt: Complete the pattern to accept order- followed by one or more digits.
explanation: The fixed prefix identifies an order. The digit class matches its numeric identifier; the end anchor prevents trailing letters.
hint: Reuse the digit class and one-or-more quantifier.

subject: regex
title: Repair a filename pattern
prompt: Repair this pattern so it accepts only the literal filename app.log.
explanation: An unescaped dot matches almost any single character. Escaping it with a backslash makes it a literal period.
hint: Escape the period.

subject: regex
title: Accept two spellings
prompt: Complete the pattern to accept color and colour, with no other letters.
explanation: ? makes the preceding token optional: zero or one u. It does not allow two u characters.
hint: Which quantifier allows zero or one?

subject: regex
title: Require a four-digit PIN
prompt: Complete the pattern to accept exactly four ASCII digits.
explanation: {4} repeats the digit token exactly four times. Anchors require the whole string to have that shape.
hint: Use a digit class with a fixed repetition count.

subject: regex
title: Choose cat or dog
prompt: Write a pattern that accepts only the complete lowercase words cat or dog.
explanation: A group keeps the alternatives together so the start and end anchors apply to both choices. ^cat|dog$ would anchor the two alternatives differently.
hint: Group the alternatives, then anchor the group.

subject: regex
title: Recognize a six-digit color
prompt: Complete the pattern to accept # followed by exactly six hexadecimal digits. Letters may be uppercase or lowercase.
explanation: Hexadecimal uses digits 0–9 and letters A–F. The character class permits both cases; {6} requires six characters.
hint: Build a character class for hexadecimal, then repeat it six times.

subject: regex
title: Validate a small identifier
prompt: Match identifiers that start with an ASCII letter or underscore, then contain zero or more ASCII letters, digits, or underscores.
explanation: The first character has a stricter class because digits cannot lead. * allows the remaining part to be empty, so a one-character name works.
hint: Use one character class for the first character and another for the rest.

subject: regex
title: Check a date-shaped string
prompt: Match exactly YYYY-MM-DD using digits in each position. Check the shape only, not whether the date exists.
explanation: Fixed-width digit groups and literal hyphens describe a shape. A regex this simple intentionally accepts impossible dates such as 2026-99-99.
hint: Use three fixed-width groups: four, two, and two digits.

subject: regex
title: Allow a controlled tag
prompt: Match exactly <b>, <i>, or <em>, including the angle brackets. Closing tags and other names must fail.
explanation: The angle brackets are literal here. A grouped alternation limits the name to the three allowed values. This is a small pattern exercise, not a general HTML parser.
hint: Put the three names in an alternative group inside the brackets.

subject: regex
title: Reject spaces in a token
prompt: Complete the pattern to accept one or more characters that are neither whitespace nor @.
explanation: Inside a character class, a leading ^ negates the class. \s covers whitespace, and @ is excluded explicitly. + rejects the empty string.
hint: Use a negated character class followed by +.

subject: python

subject: python
